# Introduction

This project examines the relationship between psychiatric symptoms and diagnostic classifications using a synthetic mental health dataset. The dataset contains binary indicators representing symptoms and diagnostic criteria associated with five psychiatric disorders: bipolar disorder, schizophrenia, depression, anxiety disorders, and post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD).

The primary aim is to explore how symptom patterns relate to diagnostic outcomes and to demonstrate how statistical and computational methods can be used to investigate these relationships. Specifically, the project addresses three questions: (1) How strongly are individual symptoms associated with their corresponding diagnoses and with other psychiatric diagnoses? (2) To what extent do different diagnoses co-occur in the dataset? (3) How do symptom counts and diagnostic thresholds influence the likelihood of meeting the dataset's diagnostic classification rules?

To address these questions, the project combines data preparation and validation, rule-based diagnostic classification, statistical association tests, and graphical visualisations. An interactive component is also planned to allow users to explore selected aspects of the data or classification rules.

Importantly, the dataset is synthetically generated, and its diagnostic indicators follow predefined rules. Consequently, the analyses primarily demonstrate computational and statistical relationships within the simulated data rather than providing empirical evidence about symptom distributions, diagnostic validity, or comorbidity in clinical populations.

# Dataset

The dataset was obtained from Kaggle (Karanbakshi1, n.d.).
The dataset (Mentalillness.csv, Kaggle) contains 3,753 synthetic participants
with 53 binary DSM-5 symptoms and criteria (0 = absent, 1 = present) and 5
binary diagnoses: bipolar disorder, schizophrenia, depression, anxiety
disorder, and PTSD. It is stored in the `data` folder.

Because the original column names are long, we first build a variable key that
gives each column a short name and records which disorder and DSM-5 criterion
it belongs to. The key is saved as `data/variable_key.csv`. We then load the
data with these short names and check that every value is 0 or 1.

```{r load-data}
source("src/r/functions_data.R")
source("src/r/functions_variable_key.R")

variable_key <- make_variable_key()
save_variable_key(variable_key, "data/variable_key.csv")
clindata <- load_mental_illness("data/Mentalillness.csv", variable_key)

knitr::kable(head(variable_key, 10))
```

## DSM rules

The diagnoses in the dataset follow fixed counting rules. The script
`test_dsm_rules.R` rebuilds all five diagnoses from the symptom columns
(with `apply_dsm_rules()`) and checks them in two ways.

```{r dsm-checks, include = FALSE}
source("src/r/test_dsm_rules.R")
```

First, it checks that the rebuilt diagnoses match the diagnoses in the data
for every participant.

```{r dsm-rule-check}
knitr::kable(rule_check)
```

### Tests

Second, it tests the rules on made-up participants placed exactly at a
cutoff (or just below it), whose diagnosis we know in advance. This is where
mistakes like `>` instead of `>=` would show up.

```{r dsm-tests}
knitr::kable(test_results)
```


# Dataset overview


```{r dataset-summary, echo=FALSE}
dataset_overview <- data.frame(
  Characteristic = c(
    "Number of participants",
    "Total number of variables",
    "Symptom and diagnostic criterion variables",
    "Diagnostic indicators",
    "Missing values",
    "Dataset type"
  ),
  Value = c(
    nrow(clindata),
    ncol(clindata),
    nrow(variable_key) - 5,
    5,
    sum(is.na(clindata)),
    "Synthetic"
  )
)

knitr::kable(
  dataset_overview,
  caption = "Overview of the mental health dataset"
)
```
The dataset contains 3,753 synthetic participant records. Individual symptoms and diagnostic criteria are represented using binary variables, with 0 indicating absence and 1 indicating presence. Diagnostic indicators identify whether each participant meets the corresponding classification rules.

The original variable names are mapped to shorter, standardised names using a variable key. This facilitates reproducible data processing and statistical analysis while preserving the correspondence between variables and their original descriptions.

Because the dataset was generated synthetically, its distributions and diagnostic relationships should not be interpreted as representative of clinical populations.

# Interactive component

The project includes an interactive Shiny application, implemented in `Shiny_Sim.Rmd`, designed to help users explore symptom profiles and diagnostic classifications within the synthetic dataset.

Users can select an individual dataset row to view its corresponding diagnostic indicators and symptom profile. Symptoms are organised by psychiatric disorder and diagnostic criterion, with visual indicators distinguishing present and absent symptoms. The application also provides expandable sections intended for reference information about diagnostic criteria.

The application uses the same data-processing and DSM-style classification functions as the statistical analyses, helping maintain consistency between the project's computational components.

**Current functionality and limitations.** The initial prototype displays the selected participant's recorded symptoms and reconstructed diagnostic labels. Although symptom indicators are presented as interactive controls, changing them does not yet recalculate diagnostic classifications. A future version will allow users to modify symptoms and compare the resulting classifications with the original dataset labels while keeping the diagnostic thresholds fixed.

The application is intended exclusively as an educational demonstration of simplified, rule-based classification using synthetic data. It is not a clinical diagnostic tool.

To explore the interactive component, open `Shiny_Sim.Rmd` in RStudio and run the application code. Additional setup instructions are provided in the repository's `README.md`.

# Statistical analysis

The script `analyses.R` runs the tests and `plots.R` makes the figures.

```{r analyses, include = FALSE}
source("src/r/analyses.R")
source("src/r/plots.R")
```

## Worked example

To show how each test works, we test whether depressed mood is related to a
depression diagnosis. A chi-square test compares the observed counts with the
counts expected if the two were unrelated; phi gives the size of the relation.

```{r worked-example}
example_table
example_test
round(example_phi, 3)
```

Depressed mood was related to a depression diagnosis, χ²(1) = 284.84,
p < .001, φ = .28.

## Symptoms and diagnoses

We repeated this test for every symptom against every diagnosis
(53 × 5 = 265 tests) and corrected the p-values for multiple testing (FDR).

```{r symptom-summary}
knitr::kable(association_summary)
```

```{r symptom-heatmap, fig.height = 10, fig.width = 7}
heatmap_plot
```

37 of 53 symptoms were related to their own diagnosis, and none of the 212
symptom–other-diagnosis pairs were related. Each diagnosis depends only on its
own symptoms. The 16 non-significant symptoms are all PTSD symptoms: PTSD needs
all eight criteria at once, so a single symptom barely changes the odds.

## Comorbidity

For every pair of diagnoses, we compared how many participants have both with
how many would have both by chance.

```{r comorbidity}
knitr::kable(comorbidity, digits = 3)
comorbidity_plot
```

No pair co-occurred more or less often than expected by chance (all FDR
p > .31). Comorbidity in this dataset is pure chance, unlike in real clinical
data.

## Symptom count and diagnosis

```{r count-steps, fig.height = 6, fig.width = 8}
steps_plot
```

For bipolar and depression, the proportion diagnosed jumps from 0 to 1 exactly
at the cutoff. For anxiety it levels off at about .50, because the diagnosis
also needs the 6-month duration item, which half of participants have. For
schizophrenia it rises gradually, because a positive symptom is also needed.
The dip at 6 anxiety symptoms reflects chance in a small group (n = 66).

# Discussion

The present project investigated symptom–diagnosis associations, diagnostic comorbidity, and symptom-count thresholds using a synthetic mental health dataset. By combining statistical analyses, rule-based classification, and visualisations, the project demonstrated how computational methods can be used to explore relationships between psychiatric symptoms and diagnostic outcomes. However, the findings must be interpreted within the context of the dataset's predefined classification rules rather than as empirical evidence concerning psychiatric disorders.

## Symptom–diagnosis associations

Following false discovery rate (FDR) correction, 37 of the 53 symptom variables showed statistically significant associations with their corresponding diagnoses, whereas none of the 212 cross-disorder comparisons reached statistical significance. These findings are consistent with the dataset's structure, in which each diagnostic indicator is determined by its associated symptom variables. Consequently, the within-disorder associations are partly inherent to the classification process rather than independently discovered relationships.

The absence of statistically significant cross-disorder associations may similarly reflect how the synthetic dataset was generated. In clinical populations, psychiatric disorders frequently share symptoms, risk factors, and underlying mechanisms (Caspi & Moffitt, 2018). Therefore, the present findings should not be interpreted as evidence that psychiatric symptoms are disorder-specific or that transdiagnostic processes are absent.

Notably, the 16 within-disorder comparisons that did not reach statistical significance involved PTSD-related variables. This finding illustrates how the relationship between an individual symptom and an overall diagnostic classification depends on the structure of the classification rule. PTSD requires the simultaneous satisfaction of several criteria, meaning that the presence of an individual symptom may be insufficient to predict the final diagnosis when other necessary conditions are unmet.

## Diagnostic comorbidity

The analyses found no statistically significant associations between the ten pairs of diagnoses after FDR correction (all adjusted *p* values above .31). The observed co-occurrence frequencies were generally close to those expected under statistical independence.

However, the absence of statistically significant results does not establish that the diagnoses are independent. Rather, the analyses did not provide sufficient evidence to reject independence within this dataset (Altman & Bland, 1995). Furthermore, the synthetic nature of the data limits the applicability of these findings to clinical populations, where psychiatric comorbidity is well documented (Kessler et al., 2005). Such comorbidity may reflect shared vulnerabilities, overlapping symptoms, or common underlying psychopathological processes (Caspi & Moffitt, 2018).

## Symptom counts and diagnostic thresholds

The symptom-count visualisations demonstrated how different classification rules produce distinct patterns. Bipolar disorder and depression displayed sharp increases in diagnostic classification at their respective symptom-count thresholds. In contrast, anxiety and schizophrenia showed more gradual patterns because classification additionally depended on duration or specific symptom requirements.

These findings illustrate that diagnostic classification cannot always be reduced to the total number of symptoms. The presence of particular symptoms, combinations of criteria, and additional conditions can be equally important. The successful reconstruction of diagnostic labels across all 3,753 records further demonstrated that the implemented functions consistently reproduce the dataset's predefined rules. Nevertheless, agreement with these rules should not be confused with clinical diagnostic validity.

## Limitations and future directions

The principal limitation of this project is its reliance on synthetic data. Because the diagnostic indicators are generated through predetermined rules, the findings primarily demonstrate the consequences of those rules rather than naturally occurring psychopathological relationships. Moreover, binary symptom coding does not capture clinically relevant differences in symptom severity, frequency, or functional impairment beyond the limited criteria explicitly represented in the dataset.

A further limitation concerns the interpretation of statistical significance. Although multiple-testing correction reduces the risk of false-positive findings, nonsignificant results do not demonstrate the absence of associations (Altman & Bland, 1995). Consequently, the present results should be interpreted as illustrations of the dataset's computational properties rather than as evidence about clinical populations.

Future developments could incorporate more realistic symptom distributions, correlated risk factors, and overlapping diagnostic presentations. The interactive Shiny application could also be extended to allow users to modify individual symptom profiles and observe how diagnostic classifications change under fixed rules. Such functionality would provide a more intuitive demonstration of the computational mechanisms underlying classification.

Overall, the project illustrates the value of reproducible programming, statistical validation, and interactive visualisation for understanding rule-based diagnostic systems, while highlighting the importance of distinguishing computational demonstrations from clinically generalisable findings.

# References

Altman, D. G., & Bland, J. M. (1995). Statistics notes: Absence of evidence is not evidence of absence. *BMJ, 311*(7003), 485. https://doi.org/10.1136/bmj.311.7003.485

Caspi, A., & Moffitt, T. E. (2018). All for one and one for all: Mental disorders in one dimension. *American Journal of Psychiatry, 175*(9), 831–844. https://doi.org/10.1176/appi.ajp.2018.17121383

Karanbakshi1. (n.d.). *Mental illness dataset* [Data set]. Kaggle. https://www.kaggle.com/datasets/karanbakshi1/mental-illness-dataset

Kessler, R. C., Chiu, W. T., Demler, O., Merikangas, K. R., & Walters, E. E. (2005). Prevalence, severity, and comorbidity of 12-month DSM-IV disorders in the National Comorbidity Survey Replication. *Archives of General Psychiatry, 62*(6), 617–627. https://doi.org/10.1001/archpsyc.62.6.617
